I was sitting on my bed with the algebra worksheet half under my thigh, pen uncapped, not writing. Cara had her knee against mine. Warm. She had been doodling a box in the margin for ten minutes and not filling it in.

"Mr. Hale did it again," she said. "Called on me like he could see I wasn't listening. I blanked so hard my face went hot."

"You always blank when a guy looks at you too long."

She snorted. "Shut up. You do too."

I did. Third period. The boy behind me. His voice dropped when he asked for a pen and I pressed my thighs together under the desk and pretended I had to pee. I didn't tell her that part. I picked at a loose thread on my shorts instead.

If I tell her the pen thing she'll laugh. If I tell her I got wet she'll want details. I don't have details. Just a voice and my thighs.

We did a little of the actual homework. Slope. A word problem about two trains that neither of us cared about. They hadn't left together. Mom was at her sister's and staying there, home by nine if she didn't get talked into another glass. Dad had the grocery run. He should have been back already. He wasn't. The house had that empty afternoon sound, fridge humming, somebody's dog two yards over. Cara was close enough that I could smell her. Skin, warm, not a product. I liked it. I had liked it for years. That was allowed.

"That girl in chem," Cara said. "The one with the hickey. She tried to cover it with concealer and it just looked like a bruise. People were so mean."

"People are always mean if they can tell you wanted it."
